results.result: More than a third (33.1%) of mouse V1 neurons exhibit color-opponent responses in their receptive field center, with the color axis explaining 33% of variance in the RF center. In contrast, the RF surround predominantly captures luminance contrast, with the luminance axis explaining 82% of variance in the surround.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C12, C14, C15 provide converging quantitative evidence from PCA analysis showing substantial color-opponency in RF centers (33% variance explained by color axis, 33.1% of neurons color-opponent). Claims C2 and C13 demonstrate surround responses are dominated by luminance (82% variance). The experimental design using center-surround color noise stimuli with appropriate controls (C72, C74) supports these findings.

results.result: Color-opponency is significantly more pronounced in posterior V1 (encoding the upper visual field) compared to anterior V1 (encoding the lower visual field). The color axis explains 39% of variance in posterior V1 versus only 19% in anterior V1, with significantly higher decoding discriminability for color in posterior regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C24, and C86 provide consistent quantitative evidence showing twice as much color variance explained in posterior versus anterior V1. Claim C25 confirms this with independent decoding analysis. The findings are reproducible across animals (C2—figure supplement 1b) and align with natural scene statistics (C26).

results.result: The asymmetry in color representations across cortex is explained by an uneven distribution of response types. Green-On/UV-Off color-opponent types are almost exclusively confined to posterior V1 (explaining 73% of variance), while green-Off/UV-On types are uniformly distributed across V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C34 provide quantitative evidence from unsupervised clustering (GMM with 89.2% assignment accuracy, C28) showing differential distribution of response types. The finding that green-On/UV-Off types are posterior-enriched while green-Off/UV-On types are evenly distributed (C31) mechanistically explains the overall asymmetry. Results are consistent across animals (C29).

results.result: Computational modeling suggests that green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types may enhance detection of predatory-like dark UV-objects in noisy daylight scenes by reducing responses to noise rather than increasing responses to objects.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 describe computational modeling results showing selective responses of green-On/UV-Off types. However, the model uses simplified parametric stimuli and linear-nonlinear assumptions (C93). The functional interpretation for predator detection (C6, C67) remains speculative without behavioral validation or more realistic natural scene testing. The model provides a plausible hypothesis but requires experimental verification.

results.result: The neuronal representation of color in mouse V1 greatly depends on ambient light levels, being strongest for photopic conditions that predominantly drive cone photoreceptors. Color representation decreases but remains detectable at low mesopic light levels, suggesting weak cone activation is sufficient for color extraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C21, C22, C80 provide consistent evidence across multiple light levels showing decreased color representation with reduced illumination. Claim C81 rules out signal-to-noise as the primary explanation by showing luminance decoding was unaffected. Claims C83-C84 demonstrate residual color encoding at low mesopic levels. The experimental design tested three light levels with appropriate controls.

results.result: The pronounced center color-opponency in V1 neurons cannot be solely attributed to color-opponency in retinal ganglion cell centers. At the retinal output level, the color axis explains only 12% of variance in RF centers, much lower than the 33% observed in V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C76 provide quantitative comparison using publicly available retinal data showing much lower center color-opponency in retinal ganglion cells (12%) versus V1 (33%). Claims C19-C20 appropriately interpret this as evidence for cortical processing beyond simple inheritance from retinal inputs. However, C20 acknowledges this is speculative regarding specific mechanisms.

results.result: Color-opponency in mouse V1 is at least partially mediated by comparison of cone signals (not purely cone-rod comparisons), though rods likely contribute to the observed color-opponent responses, particularly in posterior V1.
results.evaluation: Claim C43 is supported by the light-level experiments showing strongest color representation at photopic levels. Claims C44-C45 appropriately acknowledge rod contributions based on experimental conditions and prior literature. The interpretation balances data-driven conclusions with appropriate caveats about photoreceptor contributions.

results.result: For photopic light levels, neurons in mouse visual cortex strongly encode color features in their RF center, with significantly better discriminability for center versus surround stimuli. However, decoding performance is lower for color compared to luminance contrast.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79 are supported by independent decoding analysis using SVM with 10-fold cross-validation. The finding that color discriminability is lower than luminance but significantly better in center versus surround is consistent with the PCA results (C14-C15, C13). Statistical testing with Bonferroni correction was applied.

results.result: V1 neurons exhibit expected center-surround antagonism with negatively correlated center and surround responses. Posterior and anterior V1 neurons preferentially respond to UV and green stimuli respectively, consistent with retinal opsin distribution, though this asymmetry is less pronounced in the surround.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C18 describe validation of the experimental approach by recovering known properties of V1 neurons. The findings are consistent with established literature on center-surround antagonism and retinal opsin distribution (citations provided). These results support the validity of the experimental paradigm.

results.result: Unsupervised clustering identified 17 distinct functional response types in mouse V1 with high assignment accuracy (89.2%). Approximately half are sensitive to luminance contrast and evenly distributed, while others show spatial enrichment patterns consistent with retinal opsin distributions.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 establish the clustering methodology is robust (89.2% accuracy, consistent across animals). Claims C30, C88-C90 describe the identified response types and their distributions. Claim C91 provides independent validation through decoding analysis. The GMM approach with 17 components was justified by cross-validation (Figure 5—supplement 1a).

results.result: The linear ETA approach may inadequately capture stimulus selectivity of nonlinear neurons, though over 62% of neurons exhibited significant center ETAs, suggesting substantial coverage of the V1 population.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 appropriately acknowledges a methodological limitation. Claim C50 provides evidence that despite this limitation, the approach captured a substantial proportion of neurons. This represents appropriate scientific caution about method limitations while demonstrating the approach was reasonably effective.

results.result: The stronger cortical representation of color in posterior V1 may be an adaptation to efficiently encode enriched color contrast in the upper visual field of mouse natural scenes, as reported in prior studies of natural scene statistics and retinal processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C51-C52 cite prior work establishing asymmetric color contrast in natural scenes and retinal processing. Claim C87 appropriately frames the current findings as potentially adaptive, using cautious language ('might be'). The interpretation is speculative but well-grounded in prior literature and the current experimental findings.

results.result: Mice are dichromatic with UV- and green-sensitive cone photoreceptors that predominantly sample upper and lower visual fields respectively. Behavioral studies demonstrate mice can discriminate colors, at least in the upper visual field.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C11 summarize established background knowledge from cited literature. These are appropriately cited factual claims about mouse photoreceptor biology and color discrimination behavior that provide context for the study.

results.result: The experimental approach used GCaMP6s-expressing mice with two-photon calcium imaging in L2/3 of posterior and anterior V1. The center stimulus size (37.5°) was slightly larger than individual neuron RFs (26.2±4.6°), with validation showing >2/3 RF overlap for 83% of neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 describe methodological details with appropriate validation. Claim C72 provides quantitative evidence that stimulus alignment was adequate for most neurons. Claim C73 documents exclusion criteria. These methodological claims are well-supported by the described validation procedures.

results.result: Color vision in most species is mediated by comparing signals from different cone photoreceptor types. Recent work demonstrates extensive rod-cone opponency in mice, involving integration of cone center signals with rod surround signals, with similar mechanisms potentially existing in monochromatic humans.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 summarize established literature on color vision mechanisms across species. These are appropriately cited background claims from review articles and primary research that contextualize the current work.

results.result: The mouse visual system extracts color information at low mesopic light levels. Green-Off/UV-On color-opponency is equally distributed across cortex (suggesting color vision substrate across the visual field), while green-On/UV-Off opponency is confined to posterior V1 where it might aid aerial predator detection.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by experimental data at low light levels (C83-C84). Claim C47 is supported by response type distribution analysis (C31). Claim C48 appropriately uses cautious language ('might aid') for the functional interpretation, which is supported by modeling (C35-C38) but remains speculative without behavioral validation.

results.result: At the retinal level, color-opponency is largely mediated by center-surround interactions with few neurons exhibiting center color-opponency. Recent work suggests LGN color processing cannot be fully explained by retinal mechanisms, and integration of retinal center-surround signals might contribute to V1 color-opponency.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 appropriately cite prior literature on retinal and LGN color processing. Claim C57 offers a reasonable speculative interpretation connecting retinal mechanisms to V1 findings, appropriately qualified as inference. The interpretation is consistent with the comparative analysis of retinal and V1 data (C75-C76).

results.result: Color processing strategies differ across species. In primates, a small number of retinal cell types transmit color information with partial segregation in cortex (e.g., blob/inter-stripe regions). In contrast, zebrafish, birds, Drosophila, and mice show distributed color processing across many neuron types without clear segregation from other visual features.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 summarize comparative neuroscience literature on color processing strategies across species. These are appropriately cited background claims that contextualize the distributed color processing observed in mouse V1. The comparative framework is well-supported by cited literature.

results.result: Chromatic signals may facilitate extraction of specific environmental features rather than only supporting color discrimination per se. UV wavelengths aid object detection by increasing contrast, and different photoreceptor types may have evolved to reduce lighting noise. Distributed chromatic tuning might make sense if chromatic signals primarily boost contrast.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 present speculative functional interpretations supported by cited literature (C65-C66) and modeling results (C67). However, these remain hypotheses without direct behavioral or causal experimental validation. The reasoning is logical and grounded in prior work, but the claims are appropriately qualified as speculative ('may,' 'might').

results.result: Objects in sky, underwater, or snow environments are often more visible in UV than green wavelengths. Driving color-opponent neurons requires opposite polarity in UV and green channels. Functional neuron types with distinct color properties may unevenly sample visual space and serve distinct roles in visually guided behaviors like predator detection.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by cited literature. Claim C93 describes a mechanistic principle from modeling. Claims C94-C95 present speculative functional interpretations appropriately qualified with 'might' and 'suggest.' While the reasoning is logical and supported by modeling, the behavioral relevance remains untested and speculative.

results.result: More than a third (33.1%) of V1 neurons are color-opponent in their receptive field center, with the color axis explaining 33% of the variance in the RF center compared to 67% explained by the luminance axis.
results.evaluation: All reviewers affirm the existence and characterization of color opponency in V1. Reviewers state the paper 'provides evidence for the existence of color opponency in a subset of neurons within V1' and describe it as a 'solid characterization of the color properties of V1.' No concerns are raised about these quantitative findings.

results.result: The receptive field surround predominantly captures luminance contrast, with the luminance axis explaining 82% of variance in the RF surround and color discriminability being 40-60% lower in the surround compared to the center.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. The characterization of center-surround differences is part of the 'solid characterization' noted by reviewers, and no concerns are raised about the surround properties or the quantitative differences between center and surround.

results.result: Color-opponency is especially pronounced in posterior V1 (upper visual field), where the color axis explains 39% of variance compared to only 19% in anterior V1 (lower visual field), driven by an uneven distribution of green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating the paper 'shows that these color opponent neurons are more numerous in the upper visual field' and that 'diversity in color opponent responses exists across the visual field, with green ON/UV OFF responses more strongly represented in the upper visual field.' This is treated as a key contribution.

results.result: The neuronal representation of color greatly depends on ambient light levels, being most prominent at photopic levels and decreasing at mesopic conditions, indicating color-opponency is at least partially mediated by cone-cone comparisons rather than purely cone-rod comparisons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm this finding, noting that 'opponent responses are more pronounced at photopic light levels.' The light-level dependency is accepted as part of the characterization without challenge or concern.

results.result: Unsupervised clustering revealed distinct functional response types with different spatial distributions: green-Off/UV-On types are uniformly distributed across V1, while green-On/UV-Off types are almost exclusively confined to posterior V1, where the color axis explains 73% of variance compared to only 17% for anterior-enriched types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the clustering analysis and spatial distribution findings. One reviewer notes 'Clustering of responses revealed a set of functional cell-types based on their preference to different combinations of green and UV' and that these 'were demonstrated to have different spatial distributions across V1.' The methodology and conclusions are accepted.

results.result: Green-On/UV-Off color-opponent response types may enhance detection of predatory-like dark UV-objects in noisy daylight scenes by reducing neuronal activation to noise rather than increasing responses to objects, potentially serving a distinct role in visually guided behavior like predator detection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the modeling work and its functional interpretation. One reviewer states 'Modelling work suggests that these neurons likely support the detection of predator-like objects in the sky' and notes it provides 'insight into the ethological relevance of color opponent neurons in V1.' The speculative nature is acknowledged but the evidence is deemed convincing.

results.result: The pronounced center color-opponency in V1 neurons cannot be solely attributed to retinal ganglion cell color-opponency and likely depends on integration of both center and surround retinal signals, as the color axis explained only 12% of variance at the retinal level compared to 33% in V1.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this comparative analysis and mechanistic interpretation without challenge. While one reviewer notes 'It is unfortunate the authors were unable to provide stronger mechanistic insights,' this is framed as a limitation for future work rather than a critique of the presented comparison and inference.

results.result: The stronger cortical representation of color in posterior V1 might be an adaptation to efficiently encode the enriched color contrast in the upper visual field of mouse natural scenes, as demonstrated in previous studies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this interpretation linking the findings to natural scene statistics. One reviewer notes the work is 'argued to be relevant for the detection of certain features that are more salient when using chromatic space.' The connection to ethological relevance is treated as a strength of the study.

results.result: Methodological validation shows that despite limitations of the linear ETA approach for nonlinear neurons, over 62% of neurons exhibited significant ETAs and 83% had more than two-thirds of their center RF overlapping with the stimulus, suggesting substantial capture of V1 neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the methodological approach and validation. One reviewer notes 'The revisions have nicely clarified a few limitations of the current study, and that serves to emphasize the strengths of the data and clear conclusions that can be drawn from it.' The acknowledged limitations are treated as appropriately addressed.

results.result: Background claims about mouse photoreceptor biology, color discrimination abilities, and comparative color processing across species, including the hypothesis that chromatic signals may facilitate feature extraction rather than only color discrimination per se.
results.evaluation: These background and contextual claims are not challenged by reviewers and are treated as established knowledge appropriately cited. Reviewers focus their evaluation on the novel experimental findings rather than questioning the background framework.

results.result: Experimental methods using GCaMP6s calcium imaging in awake mice, with recordings from posterior and anterior V1 encoding upper and lower visual fields, demonstrate that V1 neurons strongly encode color features in their RF center at photopic light levels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praise the experimental approach. One states 'The large-scale single-cell resolution imaging used in this work allows the authors to map the responses of individual neurons across large regions of the visual cortex' and notes 'the dataset that forms the basis of the paper is impressive.' The methods are accepted as sound.

results.result: Clustering validation showed 89.2% assignment accuracy, all response types were present in all mice, and decoding discriminability of color was significantly better for posterior than anterior response types.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the clustering analysis and validation without challenge. The consistency across animals and the decoding results are treated as part of the convincing evidence supporting the main conclusions.

results.result: Rods likely contribute to color-opponent responses in V1, the mouse visual system extracts color information even at low mesopic light levels, and green-Off/UV-On color-opponency is equally distributed across cortex suggesting a neuronal substrate for color vision across the entire visual field.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these interpretations as part of the overall characterization. One reviewer notes the study 'provides a solid characterization of the color properties of V1' which encompasses these findings about rod contributions and spatial distribution patterns.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluations strongly support the core findings on color opponency in V1 centers (C1, C12, C14, C15). OpenEval provides detailed quantitative validation (33% variance, 33.1% color-opponent neurons), while peer reviewers affirm this as 'solid characterization' and a key contribution. Complete agreement on SUPPORTED status.

OpenEval R1 includes surround findings (C2, C13) showing luminance dominance (82% variance). Peer R2 accepts these surround properties as part of the solid characterization without challenge. Both SUPPORTED, with OpenEval providing more quantitative detail.

Both strongly support the posterior-anterior asymmetry in color processing (C3, C23, C24, C25, C86). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative evidence (twice as much color variance posteriorly) and reproducibility across animals. Peer reviewers treat this as a key contribution, explicitly affirming 'more numerous in upper visual field.' Complete agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Both support the clustering analysis and differential distribution of response types (C31, C32, C33, C34, C88, C89, C90). OpenEval emphasizes GMM methodology (89.2% accuracy) and mechanistic explanation. Peer reviewers affirm the clustering approach and spatial distribution findings. Complete agreement on SUPPORTED status.

Critical disagreement on evaluation type. OpenEval rates predator detection interpretation (C6, C35-C38, C67) as UNCERTAIN, noting model limitations and lack of behavioral validation.
